article.headline: A Software Engineer's Field Manual for the ADHD Brain
article.lede: In June 2025, Fernando Borretti — a compiler engineer in Sydney known for building *Austral*, a systems programming language — published an 8,000-word guide to managing ADHD. The article spread through an ironic relay: many readers bookmarked it immediately and never got around to it, only to return months later and discover it was, in fact, very good. The delay was an inadvertent demonstration of its thesis.
article.body:
@corsaren's tweet is itself a small illustration of the article's subject: the piece had been sitting in thousands of browser tabs since June, waiting for the long uninterrupted afternoon that never arrived. Borretti opens with an epigraph from Borges — “The pleasure is in foreseeing it, not in bringing it to term” — which he uses as a diagnostic instrument. For people with *ADHD* (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), the brain tends to reward the anticipatory imagination of a task while failing to generate the activation energy for follow-through. The article’s 8,000 words are a systematic attempt to engineer around that attractor.

The first and most uncompromising section is titled “Chemistry First.” Borretti argues that stimulant medication is the critical node in the treatment stack — the unlock without which every other intervention tends to fail. He is blunt about pill-shaming culture: “we are automata, our minds are molecules in salt water.” The **todo list** is not a productivity accessory in his framework but a *neuroprosthesis* — an external organ compensating for impaired task-oriented memory. Energy, meanwhile, he treats not as a battery but as *voltage*: highest on waking, declining through the day, with different cognitive tasks requiring different minimum thresholds. The implication is scheduling, not willpower — attack emotionally aversive tasks first and save chores for the afternoon.

Borretti distinguishes three types of procrastination that are easy to conflate but require different responses. **ADHD procrastination** — wanting to do a task but being unable to — yields to medication and system. *Anxious procrastination* — where the task triggers difficult emotions — requires cognitive-behavioral approaches and written reflection to find the emotional root. *Decision-paralysis procrastination* — too many options, unclear outcomes — calls for externalizing the problem: writing essays that treat decisions as engineering problems, or maintaining ongoing context with an AI assistant to avoid re-explaining the situation from scratch each time. The taxonomy matters because applying the wrong remedy compounds the problem.

The tactics section is the article’s most immediately practical half, and Borretti is candid that most of them are “essentially about tricking yourself.” Several stand out. *Replace interrupts with polling*: turn off all notifications and schedule a dedicated catch-up task instead, so incoming messages are processed in deliberate batches rather than as continuous interruption. *Inbox bankruptcy*: faced with an overwhelming backlog of unread messages or stale bookmarks, do not attempt heroic triage — archive everything into an “Attic” folder and start fresh. *Thrashing*, borrowed from computing (where a system spends more time swapping memory pages than doing useful work), names the pattern of a single blocked task halting all other progress; the remedy is to timebox daily effort on the blocked item while routing around it for the rest of the day.

The article appeared on Hacker News in September 2025 and drew a thread where the recurring theme was late-life diagnosis — readers in their late thirties and forties describing careers spent, in one commenter’s phrase, “going head-first through brick walls” before medication converted the effort to drywall. That reception is, in a way, the article’s most important endorsement. Written by a compiler engineer who applies the same systems-analysis lens to his own mind that he applies to programming languages, it does not ask you to try harder. It asks you to understand the system.

concepts.definition: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulty sustaining attention, regulating impulse, and initiating tasks. It has a neurological basis, and stimulant medication is its first-line pharmacological treatment.

A device or external system that compensates for a neurological deficit. Borretti uses the term to describe a todo list as a substitute for impaired working memory: rather than relying on the brain to surface tasks at the right moment, the list stores them externally and reliably.

Borretti’s metaphor for cognitive capacity: rather than a battery that depletes uniformly, he frames mental energy as voltage — a measure of what tasks are currently within reach. High-voltage states (early morning, post-medication) can power demanding or aversive work; low-voltage states can only sustain routine tasks.

A deliberate reset strategy for overwhelming message or task backlogs: rather than triaging hundreds of accumulated items, you archive everything into a holding folder and start fresh. The goal is to unblock future use of the system without requiring a heroic one-time effort.

In computing, thrashing occurs when a system spends more time managing memory swaps than doing productive work. Borretti applies the term to a productivity pattern: a single blocked task generates so much anxiety that it halts all other work. His remedy is to timebox effort on the blocked item and route the rest of the day around it.

A tactic from systems programming applied to communication: instead of allowing notifications to interrupt work as they arrive (interrupt-driven), you turn off all notifications and schedule deliberate catch-up periods (polling). This preserves focus blocks and eliminates unpredictable context switches.

One of three procrastination types Borretti identifies: the failure to act due to an excess of options or unclear outcomes, rather than emotional aversion or attention difficulties. It requires externalization strategies — writing out the decision, seeking outside perspective — rather than pharmaceutical or willpower-based interventions.
